questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'She worked hard ______ she passed the exam.'

options.option_text: but (wrong: 'but' shows contrast; working hard leading to passing is not a contrast)
so (correct: 'so' shows result/consequence; working hard → passing ✓)
although (wrong: 'although' shows contrast — would suggest she passed DESPITE something)
unless (wrong: 'unless' means 'if not'; changes the meaning completely)

questions.explanation: B is correct. SO = shows result or consequence. 'She worked hard SO she passed' = the passing was the result of working hard. CAUSE → EFFECT connectors: so, therefore, thus, hence, as a result. CONTRAST connectors: but, however, although, despite, yet.

questions.stem: Choose the correct connector: 'He is old; ______, he is very energetic.'

options.option_text: therefore (therefore shows result; old → energetic isn't a causal result)
however (correct: 'however' shows contrast; being old yet energetic is a contrast ✓)
moreover (moreover = in addition; doesn't show contrast)
consequently (consequently = as a result; not a contrast)

questions.explanation: B is correct. HOWEVER = despite what was just said; used to show contrast. 'He is old; HOWEVER, he is very energetic' = the energy is surprising given his age. Contrast connectors: however, nevertheless, nonetheless, yet, but, on the other hand, in contrast.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: '______ the rain, the match continued.'

options.option_text: Because of (wrong: 'because of the rain' would mean rain CAUSED something; the match continued despite rain)
Despite (correct: 'despite the rain' = the rain was not enough to stop the match; concessive ✓)
Since (wrong: 'since the rain' = because of the rain; suggests rain as a reason)
As (wrong: 'as the rain' = while it was raining; introduces a simultaneous clause differently)

questions.explanation: B is correct. DESPITE = in spite of; not affected or deterred by. 'Despite the rain' = the match continued even though it was raining. Concession connectors + noun/noun phrase: despite, in spite of. Concession connectors + clause: although, even though, though, while.

questions.stem: Choose the correct connector: 'He is not only intelligent ______ also hardworking.'

options.option_text: and (wrong: 'not only...and also' is not the standard construction)
but (correct: 'not only...but also' is the standard correlative conjunction pair ✓)
or (wrong: 'not only...or also' is not standard)
so (wrong: 'not only...so also' is not standard)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'NOT ONLY...BUT ALSO' is a correlative conjunction pair used to add emphasis to two elements. 'He is not only intelligent BUT ALSO hardworking.' Other correlative pairs: both...and; either...or; neither...nor; whether...or; such...that; so...that.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'I will go ______ you agree to come with me.'

options.option_text: unless (correct: 'unless you agree' = 'if you don't agree, I won't go' ✓)
until (wrong: 'until you agree' = waiting for agreement; suggests I'm waiting, not refusing)
although (wrong: 'although you agree' = despite your agreement; wrong meaning)
because (wrong: 'because you agree' = for the reason that you agree; changes meaning)

questions.explanation: A is correct. UNLESS = except if; on the condition that... doesn't happen. 'I will go UNLESS you agree to come' = I will go IF you don't agree to come. UNTIL = up to the time that (temporal). Be careful: 'unless' always introduces a negative condition, even without 'not' in the clause.

questions.stem: Choose the correct connector: 'She loves music. ______, she plays three instruments.'

options.option_text: However (wrong: however shows contrast; love of music + playing instruments is not a contrast)
In fact (correct: 'in fact' strengthens or adds evidence to the previous statement ✓)
Nevertheless (wrong: nevertheless shows contrast/concession)
Although (wrong: although shows contrast and introduces a clause, not a standalone sentence)

questions.explanation: B is correct. IN FACT = used to emphasise truth or introduce supporting evidence. 'She loves music. In fact, she plays three instruments' = the playing of instruments supports or exemplifies the love of music. Addition/emphasis connectors: in fact, indeed, moreover, furthermore, in addition, besides.

questions.stem: Identify the INCORRECTLY used conjunction: 'Although he was tired, but he continued working.'

options.option_text: The sentence is correct (wrong: using both 'although' and 'but' is a double conjunction error)
The sentence is incorrect — should be 'Although he was tired, he continued working.' (correct: 'although' alone is sufficient; 'but' is redundant ✓)
Replace 'although' with 'even if' (wrong: the error is the double conjunction, not 'although' itself)
Replace 'but' with 'yet' (wrong: 'yet' is still redundant with 'although'; remove one conjunction)

questions.explanation: B is correct. DOUBLE CONJUNCTION ERROR: 'Although...but' is incorrect because both 'although' and 'but' express contrast — using both is redundant. Use EITHER: 'Although he was tired, he continued' OR 'He was tired, but he continued.' This is one of the most common errors in Indian English exams.

questions.stem: Choose the correct conjunction: 'I have been working here ______ five years.'

options.option_text: for (correct: 'for' is used with duration; 'for five years' ✓)
since (wrong: 'since' is used with a point of time: 'since 2018', not a duration)
from (wrong: 'from five years' is incorrect; 'from' needs a starting point: 'from Monday')
during (wrong: 'during five years' is not standard; 'during the five years' = possible but unusual)

questions.explanation: A is correct. FOR + DURATION: 'for five years', 'for a long time', 'for two months.' SINCE + POINT OF TIME: 'since 2018', 'since Monday', 'since morning.' Both are typically used with perfect tenses. Memory: FOR = for a period (F for period); SINCE = from a specific starting point.

options.option_text: While I agree with you, but I think there are other factors. (wrong: 'while...but' = double conjunction error like 'although...but')
She was cooking while he watched television. (correct: 'while' = during the time that; two simultaneous actions ✓)
I finished my work while I am tired. (wrong: tense mismatch — 'while' needs same tense context)
While the game had begun, the rain started. (wrong: awkward — 'when' would be better for this sequence)

questions.explanation: B is correct. WHILE = during the time that (temporal) OR although (concessive). 'She was cooking WHILE he watched television' = two things happening simultaneously. 'While I agree' = although I agree. 'While...but' is wrong — same double conjunction error as 'although...but.'

questions.stem: Choose the correct connector to express purpose: 'He saved money ______ buy a new car.'

options.option_text: in order that (wrong: 'in order that' is followed by a clause, not an infinitive: 'in order that he could buy')
so as to (correct: 'so as to + infinitive' expresses purpose ✓; 'so as to buy')
despite (wrong: despite shows concession, not purpose)
because (wrong: because shows reason for past action, not purpose going forward)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Purpose connectors: 'SO AS TO + infinitive' and 'IN ORDER TO + infinitive' are equivalent. 'He saved money so as to buy a car' = purpose. 'In order that + clause' is for more formal contexts. 'So that + clause' = 'he saved money SO THAT he could buy a car.' 'So as to' = before the infinitive directly.
